A True Must See! Sidewinder Drops a Hardshell Camper With Sidecar Mounting for Motorcyclists
14 photos
Photo: Sidewinder Campers
For the longest time, motorcyclists had a hard time tapping into glamping mainly because there are too few campers out there that are light enough to hitch up to a motorcycle. Those that do exist and onto which we've shed light before are often pop-up solutions with soft shells. Well, one team has done it, giving birth to a lineup of hardshell campers aimed at steel steed lovers out there.
The name is Sidewinder, and if it weren’t for a Facebook ad, I would have never found out about this crew; they’re that obscure and under-the-radar, so to speak. As to what makes this crew so special, well, you clearly picked up on the fact that they craft campers for motorcycles, but how they do it and what they give rise to is clearly worth your attention.
Sidewinder breaks the mold of traditional bike campers in two ways. The first is that they give rise to a hardwall solution, and the second is by the positioning of those campers: they mount them in a sidecar position and are not towed along like you’d expect. I’m guessing you’re reading this BECAUSE of the main image you spotted.
Photo: Time Out Trailers, Inc. Overall, Sidewinder manufactures several options for bikers to tap into, but it’s the Pygmy that stands as the smallest (7 ft long, 4 ft wide) of the bunch, a proverbial flagship, so to speak, one that displays the bare bones that this brand has to offer rather than a frilled-out one. That’s also the RVing solution we’ll be tapping into today.
Now, as the smallest solution, Sidewinder crafts a camper that clearly weighs very little as it’s designed to be used in conjunction with a vehicle that is not known for its towing prowess. How little? How does 350 lbs (159 kg) sound?
Sure, it’s not as light as some softshell options out there, but it’s still good enough for some stronger bikes. Just keep in mind that because of how the camper is mounted to the frame, stresses are going to be a bit different, so a specialized frame is also called upon to mount these puppies to your ride.
Photo: Sidewinder Campers According to Sidewinder, this mounting system is good for cruise, adventure, and touring bikes. Grab your gear because the world just got a whole lot bigger.
Oh, and according to images on the manufacturer’s website, these sidecar campers can even be operated while there’s someone inside. Clearly, you’ll want to stick to tarmac as you do, but that is wild, nonetheless.
What we don’t know is the GVWR of the Pygmy, or any other camper spotted on Sidewinder’s website. I’ll be sure to update this article once I have that information.
This weight is granted by the way the Pygmy is completed which is a blend between wood, composite, and good old steel, birthing a rigid camper that can suit the needs of up to two guests and does so in a fashion very similar to teardrop campers, even going as far as being equipped with off-grid features.
Photo: Sidewinder Campers Given the compact footprint , space is clearly limited and the Pygmy is set up in a wagon-like arrangement, with spaces and features set up in a straight line. The front of the unit is reserved for nothing more than a space where the two owners have a place to rest their head, along with a water tank and battery underneath the floor, and at the rear, the galley block. Yes, this one has a kitchen too.
Honestly, what more could you want? It can even handle a solar panel, AC system, roof-rack, awning, and so much more. I can’t wait to find out the GVWR of this unique and about-damn-time option for riders. Insulated walls also help keep us exploring into a bit of the colder season; grab a good heater.
After you’ve made it to camp, wherever that may be, you’ll kick out a couple of stabilizer legs, turn on the solar panel and pump, unfurl your awning and set up the dining area or lounge, and finally, pop the rear hatch so that you can grab a cold drink, cook up dinner, and wash your hands.
Photo: Sidewinder Campers You may be asking where the dining set came from, but you probably figured out that it was probably stuffed inside the camper. Yet, there is more storage available underneath the floor, accessible from outside; ample space for gear and other systems. Sidewinder even shows off the Pygmy with an outside shower mounted to the side of the camper.
Keep in mind that the interior of the Pygmy offers a total of just four feet in height to work with, so you clearly won't be standing up inside this one, but for reading a book, escaping bad weather, resting, and cuddling, it’s perfect.
As for the question on our mind: How much can we expect to drop on a Pygmy? Well, for the time being, the Sidewinder doesn't showcase price for this unit and urges owners to simply reach out to them directly for a quote.
Photo: Sidewinder Campers However, some sources mention that their pricing starts somewhere around $10K (€9,000) for the smallest models, so we can take that into consideration since this is the smallest model this crew offers. Would you rock a Pygmy ?
Keep in mind one thing as you explore what you see here today, and it’s that Sidewinder offers very limited images of a Pygmy, so some are of other solutions from this brand, but there’s no doubt that the Pygmy can be just as equipped as some of the larger ones. Nothing changes much across the classes expect size and weight, of course.
